e.etymology: A Spanish phonetic spelling of the English pronunciation of Nathan, from Hebrew natan, 'he gave'. It spread in Spain and Latin America in the 2010s.
A Brazilian given name, apparently a variant of Hendrik or Hendrick, forms of Henry. Its US rise follows the Brazilian soccer star Endrick.
A spelling of Brendan, from Old Irish Brenainn, which goes back to a Welsh word for 'prince' or 'king'. Saint Brendan the Navigator is the best-known early bearer.

e.meaning: noble strength (as a pet form of Audrey)
e.etymology: For girls, a pet form of Audrey, from Old English Aethelthryth, 'noble strength'. The boys' name, best known from war hero Audie Murphy, is of uncertain origin, possibly a French surname.
namesakes: Audie Murphy (decorated World War II soldier and film actor)
Audie Cornish (journalist and former NPR host)

assoc.t: sounds like Audi, the German car maker

e.etymology: A double-l spelling of Maximilian, from the Roman name Maximilianus, a derivative of Maximus, 'greatest'. It reached English through German, where emperors bore it.
A spelling of Anastasia, from Greek anastasis, 'resurrection'. The name honors a 4th-century martyr and was first given to children born around Easter.

assoc.t: Anastasia, the lost Romanov princess and 1997 animated film

e.etymology: A name with several sources. Chinese Tai is often written with the character for 'great, peaceful', and Vietnamese Tai means 'talent'. In the US it is also used as a spelling of Ty.
namesakes: Tai Frasier (Brittany Murphy's character in Clueless)

e.etymology: A modern American name that joins the Ja- of Jamie and Jamal to the -iyah ending of Aaliyah.
In the US mostly a modern elaboration of Sarah and Sariah in the style of Aaliyah. There is also an Arabic name Sariyah, from a root meaning 'to travel by night'.
Yiddish Feyge, traditionally taken as 'bird' (compare Yiddish foygl) and paired with the Hebrew name Tzipporah. It is used mainly in Hasidic and other Orthodox Jewish families.
A spelling of Jayden favored by Spanish-speaking families. Jayden is a modern American name built from the sounds of Jay and Jade plus the -den ending.
A spelling of Jacqueline, the French feminine of Jacques, from Hebrew Yaakov (Jacob), who was born grasping his twin brother's heel. This form is common in Brazil and Latin America.

Three names share the spelling: the Turkish form of Arabic Umar, 'flourishing, long-lived'; Hebrew Omer, 'sheaf of grain'; and French Omer, from Germanic Audomar, 'wealth' plus 'famous', the name of Saint Omer.

assoc.t: the Omer, the 49 days counted from Passover to Shavuot

e.etymology: An elaboration of Adela and Adele, short forms of Germanic names beginning with adal, 'noble'. It was most popular in the US in the late 1800s.
Used as a first name mostly for its sound, close to Nathan and Ethan with an initial L. Lathan also exists as a surname.

The Spanish and Portuguese form of Jerome, from Greek Hieronymos: hieros, 'sacred', plus onoma, 'name'. Saint Jerome translated the Bible into Latin. The same name, spelled Geronimo, was the Apache leader's.

assoc.t: Geronimo, the Apache leader (same name, spelled with G)
Geronimo!, the shout made when jumping

e.etymology: From Sanskrit navina, 'new, fresh, young'. It is a common boys' name across India, also spelled Navin.

assoc.t: Prince Naveen in Disney's The Princess and the Frog

e.etymology: A spelling of Israel, the name given to Jacob in Genesis after he wrestles with an angel, from Hebrew Yisrael, 'he struggles with God'. The z form is standard in Polish, Czech and Hungarian.

assoc.t: Israel, the country in the Middle East

e.note: Heard first as the country, so it can carry political associations.

e.etymology: A respelling of Zaire, the former name of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and of the Congo River, from a Kikongo word for 'river'.
A modern American name. It can be read as a respelling of Jelani, an East African name usually glossed 'mighty', or as Jah- plus the Hawaiian lani, 'sky', found in Kalani and Leilani.
A modern form of the biblical Uzziah, Hebrew for 'the Lord is my strength', which appears as Ozias in older English Bibles. The -iah ending matches Josiah and Isaiah.
The Spanish form of Ephraim, from Hebrew Efrayim, 'fruitful', a son of Joseph in Genesis. It honors Saint Ephrem the Syrian, a 4th-century hymn writer.
namesakes: Efren Ramirez (actor, Pedro in Napoleon Dynamite)

e.etymology: Listed in American name books as a Swahili name meaning 'like the moon'; it goes back to Arabic qamar, 'moon'.
From Arabic Sumayya, tied to the root for 'height, elevation'. Sumayya bint Khayyat, an early convert, is honored as the first martyr of Islam.
A modern American coinage that extends Dax with the -on ending of Jaxon and Paxton.
A respelling of Haven, the English word for a harbor or place of safety, from Old English haefen.

A respelling of Wesley, now given mostly to girls. Wesley is an English place name and surname from Old English west plus leah, 'meadow, clearing', made a first name in honor of Methodist founder John Wesley.
A spelling of Alani, the Hawaiian word for the orange and its tree. It is also sometimes used as a feminine form of Alan.

assoc.t: Alani Nu, energy drink brand (spelled Alani)

e.etymology: A spelling of Arabic Yunus, the Quran's name for the prophet Jonah, from Hebrew Yonah, 'dove'.
A respelling of Lennox, the Scottish district and earldom, whose name comes from Gaelic leamhan, 'elm'. The Lynn spelling gives it a softer look.

assoc.t: sounds like Lennox, the heating and cooling brand

e.etymology: Of unclear origin as a given name. It can be a clipped form of Liam or William (singer Iam Tongi is a William) or a variant of Ian, and it also reads as the phrase I am.
e.note: Reads as the phrase 'I am' on paper and may be taken for a typo of Liam or Ian.

e.etymology: A combination of Ann, from Hebrew Channah, 'grace', and Marie, the French form of Mary. The pairing follows French Anne-Marie.
